story.name: Entry 69 | Is EdTech our Friend or Foe?

content.title: Entry 69 | Is EdTech our Friend or Foe?
content.author: Tayyab Tufayl Hussain

content.text: Welcome to the age of the one-touch button, a world where a single click can send out an emergency SOS to save a life or, paradoxically, trigger catastrophic consequences. This metaphor captures the dual nature of technological advancement: it holds immense potential to empower, yet it also carries risks. Nowhere is this more evident than in education, where digital learning and artificial intelligence (AI) are rapidly reshaping long-held philosophies and practices. Traditionally, classrooms were structured around teacher-centered instruction, rigid curricula, and textbook-based learning. Teachers were seen as the primary source of knowledge, and students were expected to absorb and reproduce that knowledge in standardized ways. Educational philosopher William C. Bagley's theory of Essentialism encapsulates this model, emphasizing discipline, core subjects, and the teacher's central authority. However, the 21st century has ushered in a new paradigm. With the rise of AI and virtual learning environments, students are no longer passive recipients. They are now active participants in their education. Digital tools allow learners to choose what they want to learn, how they want to learn it, and at what pace. Simulations, real-time feedback, personalized scaffolding, and even translation tools help make learning more accessible and inclusive. In their research, Holmes, Bialik, and Fadel (2019) highlight how AI enhances learning by providing individualized instruction tailored to students' needs. This aligns closely with Vygotsky's concept of the Zone of Proximal Development, where learners can progress further when supported by just-in-time guidance, something AI can now simulate effectively.

While Bagley resisted the shift from traditional methods, Progressivist thinkers like John Dewey advocated for experiential, student-centered learning. Dewey argued that knowledge is best constructed through doing (through exploration, social interaction, and real-world problem-solving). Today, technology enables just that. AI and virtual platforms can create immersive learning experiences that align with Dewey's philosophy, allowing students to engage meaningfully with content and context.

To explore this tension between tradition and innovation, I conducted an experiment in my classroom on April 29, 2025. Two groups of students were tasked with presenting a scene from Romeo and Juliet. Group A was provided with laptops, mobile devices, and internet access. Group B was given only printed novels and notepads. Group A created a dynamic multimedia presentation using AI-generated visuals and PowerPoint. Their presentation was quick, polished, and could be archived and reviewed later. Group B, on the other hand, performed a live theatrical scene. Their version was slower to prepare but emotionally compelling, so it gave an authentic, human-centered experience that engaged the audience in real time. This comparison raised important questions: Is efficiency more valuable than emotional depth? Can human creativity coexist with algorithmic intelligence? Should we trade the unpredictability of human learning for the precision of machine support?

The truth is, we don't have to choose one over the other. The most effective educational approach today lies in balance. We must find a middle ground between Essentialism and Progressivism, between the wisdom of tradition and the possibilities of innovation. While technology may sometimes distance us from human connection, it also empowers us to learn in ways we never imagined. It is not inherently good or bad, the value depends on how it is utilized. AI should support educators, not replace them. It should not write for us, but with us and refine, challenge, and extend our ideas rather than giving us ideas. As learners, we should first attempt to think, write, and create on our own, and then use AI to enhance that process, just as a microscope sharpens what the eye already sees. Ultimately, embracing AI in education is not about abandoning human development. It's about redefining it.

body.quote: This blog post explores the tension between traditional and digital education. The author contrasts Essentialism, which emphasizes a teacher-centered, rigid curriculum, with Progressivism, which advocates for student-centered, experiential learning. References Dewey, J. (1938). Experience and Education. New York: Macmillan. Holmes, W., Bialik, M., & Fadel, C. (2019). Artificial Intelligence in Education: Promises and Implications for Teaching and Learning. Boston: Center for Curriculum Redesign. Luckin, R., Holmes, W., Griffiths, M., & Forcier, L. B. (2016). Intelligence Unleashed: An Argument for AI in Education. Pearson Education.

body.title: About the
body.bio: ​About the Author Tayyab Hussain is an English instructor and an MPhil Education scholar from the class of 2026 at AKU IED, Pakistan. Beyond classroom teaching, he has a real appetite for learning modern Ed-tech tools to create interactive learning environments. He believes in the power of a one-touch button world, but at the same time, he suggests to use a balanced approach between technological and analog education systems. ​
